lines.text: A car drives up a wall, until it's hanging almost upside down. Tesla really did this. So why doesn't it fall?
At the reveal of the new Roadster, the car drove up a giant curved ramp, and clung to it, nearly upside down.
Normally, tires grip because the car's weight presses them into the road. Upside down, that weight pulls the wrong way.
So Tesla built a vacuum into the car. Fans at the back suck the air out from underneath.
Skirts drop down along the sides to seal the gap, so the air can't rush back in.
Now the air under the car is thinner than the air around it. So the atmosphere itself pushes the car onto the surface.
Tesla's screen showed about forty-seven hundred kilos of downforce. Far more than the car weighs. So it sticks, even upside down.
And unlike wings, fans work even when the car is slow, or standing still.
The idea isn't new. Race cars tried fans decades ago, and racing banned them for being too good.
Then it jumped. Thrusters blasting compressed air lifted it right off the ground.
Tesla claims zero to sixty in under one second, and production in twenty twenty-eight. Those are Tesla's own numbers, not tested yet.
